entities.name: Marcus Peducaeus Stloga Priscinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Peducaeus Stloga Priscinus ascended to the pinnacle of Roman senatorial ambition, serving as an ordinary consul in 141 CE, a crucial period during the stable reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius. His career exemplifies the structured progression through the *cursus honorum* that defined the political lives of the Roman elite in the mid-second century AD. As a member of the venerable Peducaea gens, his public service underscored the enduring influence of established Roman families within the imperial administration, even as the power of the emperor grew.

Priscinus's most significant achievement was his ordinary consulship, which he held alongside Titus Hoenius Severus. This annual office, while largely ceremonial by the second century, remained the highest honor in the Roman Republic's legacy, marking the year in official documents and providing immense prestige. During his tenure, Priscinus would have presided over the Senate, overseen public festivals, and performed various civic duties, solidifying his position within the ruling class of the vast Roman Empire. His active service during the Antonine peace reflects a period of efficient governance and relative internal tranquility.

His career, though not marked by dramatic military campaigns or legislative reforms, contributes to our understanding of the routine yet vital functioning of the Roman state during its zenith. Priscinus's participation in the imperial administration helped maintain the vast infrastructure and legal framework that governed millions, ensuring the continuity of Roman authority across three continents. His life reflects the stability and institutional strength that characterized the Antonine Age, laying the groundwork for subsequent generations of Roman leaders.
